# The Rabbit Comes Out of the Hole

Someone hands you a length of rope and asks you to tie a bowline. You have never tied one. They explain: make a small loop in the standing part, pass the working end up through the loop, around behind the standing part, and back down through the loop. Every word of that is English. You understand each one. And what you produce, almost certainly, is a sad lump that falls apart when you pull on it.

Then they take the rope back and do it in one second, and you see nothing. They do it again slowly and you see a blur with a beginning and an end. Eventually they teach you the mnemonic — the rabbit comes out of the hole, runs around the tree, and goes back down the hole — and something about that absurd little story does what the precise geometric description could not. You get it. Not intellectually. Your hands get it, which is a different organ of understanding, and one that language reaches only by accident and indirection.

I find this genuinely strange. The bowline is not complicated. It has maybe four steps. It can be drawn, photographed, animated, described in prose, encoded as a sequence of crossings. And still the reliable transmission channel is a person, a rope, and a nonsense rhyme about a rabbit. Knowledge that lives in the fingers and passes between bodies has a different physics than knowledge that lives in sentences. Most of what humans know how to do is like this. We just don't notice, because the parts we can write down are the parts we've learned to talk about.

---

Clifford Ashley noticed. He was a painter from New Bedford, Massachusetts, a decent impressionist who had gone on a whaling voyage as a young man and come back with a subject he could not put down. He painted sailors, he wrote about the whale fishery, and then sometime in the 1920s he started drawing knots. Eleven years later he published *The Ashley Book of Knots*: 3,854 numbered entries, around seven thousand illustrations, and an index that itself requires study. It came out in 1944, into a world that had almost finished with rope. Steam and steel had taken the merchant fleets; the working sail was going; the great vocabulary of hitches and bends and seizings that had accumulated over five thousand years of hauling things was about to become folklore. Ashley wrote with the urgency of a man recording a language whose last fluent speakers were retiring.

What strikes me about the book is not its completeness but its taxonomy, which is stricter than casual usage suggests. A knot, properly, is a thing tied in a rope that holds by itself — a stopper, a loop. A hitch is tied *around* something and would dissolve without it; you cannot show someone a clove hitch in isolation, because the spar is part of the knot. A bend joins two ropes. A splice is not a knot at all, and we'll come back to that. A lashing binds objects together. There are also seizings, whippings, sennits, Turk's heads, and a whole sub-discipline of decorative work that sailors made in the endless idle hours of long passages, which is to say that a significant fraction of this technical literature is art produced by bored men on the night watch.

The precision is not pedantry. Ashley was scathing about the reef knot — the square knot, the one everybody knows, the one on every bandage and every shoelace — because people use it to join ropes, and it is bad at joining ropes. Under the wrong load it capsizes: the two loops flip and the thing spills. Tie it slightly wrong and you have a granny knot, which is worse, and which a distressing number of surgeons tie without knowing it, in a body, with suture material slick enough that the difference matters. Studies have been done on this. The results are not flattering to the profession. There is a whole small literature of surgical knot security, full of terms like *knot slippage* and *loop-to-security failure*, which is a very polite way of saying the thing came undone inside someone.

---

Here is the fact about rope that I think is the most beautiful thing in this entire subject, and almost nobody knows it.

Wrap a line around a fixed post. Hold one end. Let the load pull on the other. The friction between rope and post does not add up linearly with the amount of contact — it compounds. Each tiny arc of wrap squeezes the rope against the post slightly harder, which increases the friction on the next tiny arc, which squeezes harder still. The relationship is exponential. The capstan equation says the holding force equals your force multiplied by *e* raised to the coefficient of friction times the total angle of wrap.

Run the numbers. With a modest friction coefficient of 0.3 and three full turns around a bollard, the multiplier is roughly 285. You pull with one pound; the rope holds two hundred and eighty-five. Add a fourth turn and you're near two thousand. This is why a dockhand who weighs a hundred and sixty pounds can stop a ship that weighs ten thousand tons, by taking a few turns around a post and holding the tail. It looks like a magic trick. It is a magic trick performed by the number *e*, which apparently was waiting in the rope the whole time.

The same exponential is why a belay device works, why you can arrest a falling climber with one hand, why a rope wrapped twice around a tree branch will hold a truck. Nature has very few gifts like this — places where a small linear input buys an enormous output — and one of them is sitting in the physics of a string wrapped around a stick. Sailors knew it in their bodies for millennia before anyone wrote the equation. The knowledge was correct, useful, and completely opaque. They just knew that another turn was worth a great deal more than the last one.

---

And yet a knot always weakens the rope. Always. There is no knot that leaves the line at full strength.

The reason is curvature. Where the rope bends sharply, the fibers on the outside of the bend travel a longer path and take a disproportionate share of the load, while the fibers on the inside go slack. The load stops being shared and starts being concentrated. A typical knot costs you somewhere between a fifth and a half of the rope's rated breaking strength. The rope will fail at the knot, essentially every time, which means the knot is simultaneously the thing making the rope useful and the thing that will kill you.

This is a fairly exact description of a lot of engineering, and of a lot of other things too. The connection point is the weak point. The place where you join is the place where it breaks. You cannot have a rope that does anything without putting a knot in it, and every knot you put in makes it less of a rope.

Ashley's answer to this — the sailor's answer, the ancient answer — is the splice, and I want to hold that in reserve for the end, because it is the only genuinely hopeful thing in the subject.

---

Meanwhile, the word has been busy.

A *knot* is a unit of speed because sailors measured speed by throwing a wooden chip off the bow, attached to a line with knots tied at regular intervals, and counting how many knots ran out through their fingers while a sandglass emptied. Twenty-eight seconds. Knots spaced forty-seven feet three inches apart. Do the arithmetic and you get nautical miles per hour. So every time a pilot says *two hundred and fifty knots*, they are using a word that means, literally, *how many bumps in a string went past my hand*. The technology is gone. The rope is gone. The sandglass is gone. The counting survives inside the number.

And then there is *dénouement*.

It comes from the French *nouer*, to tie, from the Latin *nodus*. A *dénouement* is an untying. The plot is understood, by the language itself, to be a knot — the threads pulled into tension, crossed, snarled — and the ending is not a resolution or a conclusion but specifically an *untying*, the working end finally pulled back through the loop. Horace, giving advice to playwrights, wrote that a god should not intervene in a story unless the knot has become worthy of such an untyer. *Nec deus intersit, nisi dignus vindice nodus.* He is treating narrative difficulty as a physical object with a tensile rating. Don't bring in the crane unless the rope is genuinely tight.

I love that the metaphor was already dead when Horace used it. It is dead in every language that has it. Nobody says "the untying of that film was unsatisfying." The knot has been forgotten inside the word, the way the sandglass has been forgotten inside the speed.

---

Mathematicians took the knot literally and it turned out to be enormous.

A mathematical knot is a closed loop in three-dimensional space — take the string, tie whatever you like, then fuse the ends so nothing can slip off. The question is whether two such loops are the same, meaning: can you deform one into the other without cutting? You're allowed to push, pull, stretch, and pass the loop through itself in projection, but never to break it.

The simplest knot is the *unknot*, a plain circle. Recognizing it should be easy. It is not easy. It is one of those problems that looks like it should take ten minutes and instead took sixty years and several Fields Medals' worth of machinery. Haken gave an algorithm in 1961. Complexity theorists proved the problem is in NP — if someone hands you a solution you can check it efficiently — while nobody could find a fast general method, and the best bounds on how many moves you might need were exponential in the number of crossings.

The genuinely upsetting part is this: there exist diagrams of the unknot that cannot be simplified without first being made *more complicated*. You have a hundred-crossing tangle that is, in truth, a circle, and every available simplifying move is a dead end. To get out, you must add crossings. You must make the mess worse before it can get better, and there is no local signal telling you which worsening is the right one.

I don't want to over-read this. But I have never been able to stop reading it. Anyone who has ever tried to think their way out of a bad situation knows the shape of it: the moves that feel like progress are all unavailable, and the only route runs through something that looks, from inside, like making it worse. Mathematics has produced a rigorous, unarguable diagram of that experience. It is called the hard unknot. There are papers about it with pictures.

The best recent story in the field is Lisa Piccirillo's. In 2020 she settled the Conway knot problem: an eleven-crossing knot that John Conway had found as a young man in the 1950s, whose *sliceness* — a subtle four-dimensional property — had resisted everyone for fifty years. Piccirillo heard about it at a workshop as a graduate student, thought about it for about a week, and solved it. Her method was a lateral move rather than a frontal assault: she found a different knot that shares the Conway knot's "trace," a four-dimensional object built from it, and sliceness is invariant under that sharing. So she computed something about the *other* knot, where the tools happened to work, and the answer transferred. She didn't untie it. She found something that was tied the same way in the relevant respect and untied that instead.

Which is, if you think about it, exactly the sort of thing you do with a real knot when the end is buried: you stop pulling and you look at it from a different angle.

---

Now the part that made me want to write about any of this.

Your DNA is about two meters long per cell, packed into a nucleus a few microns across, and it is a closed loop in many contexts, and it is being constantly unzipped, copied, and read. It gets knotted. Not metaphorically — actually, topologically knotted, and supercoiled, and catenated with its sister chromosomes after replication like two interlocked rubber bands. A cell that cannot untangle its DNA cannot divide. It just stops, or dies.

So there are enzymes whose entire job is untying. Topoisomerases. They work by cutting. Type II topoisomerase grabs a double helix, cleaves both strands, holds the broken ends in a protein clamp so they cannot escape, passes another duplex through the gap, and reseals the break. It is a stage magician's trick performed several times a second in essentially every cell of your body, and it is the only way through, because topology does not care about your intentions. You cannot untie a closed loop by wishing. You must cut it.

Life, at its most fundamental, is a knot-tying and knot-untying operation, and the unknotting requires a controlled, temporary, reversible break in the thing that defines you.

Which is why some of our best chemotherapy drugs are topoisomerase *poisons*. Etoposide, the camptothecins, irinotecan — they don't block the enzyme. They let it cut, and then they trap it in the cut state, wedged in the moment of breakage, unable to reseal. The cell's own unknotting machinery becomes a source of permanent double-strand breaks, and the cell, which is dividing fast, dies of it. Ciprofloxacin does the analogous thing to bacterial gyrase. We have built an entire pharmacology out of the observation that a thing which must cut itself to survive can be killed by being prevented from healing.

There is no lesson here that isn't obvious and slightly awful. The vulnerability is not separable from the capability. The enzyme that saves the cell is the enzyme that kills it, depending only on whether the last step completes.

---

The Inca kept their accounts in string.

A khipu is a primary cord with pendant cords hanging from it, sometimes hundreds, sometimes with subsidiary cords hanging off those, in a hierarchy. Knots in the pendants encode numbers, positionally, in base ten — figure-eights for ones, long knots with a variable number of turns for the digits two through nine, single knots for the higher powers, and empty space for zero. So does the wedding ring, so does the string around the finger, so does the yellow ribbon, so does the *nodus* on the phylactery.

Alexander, at Gordium, was told that whoever untied the knot binding the yoke to the pole of an old ox-cart would rule Asia. He looked at it for a while and then cut it in half with his sword.

Fewer remember that Aristobulus, who was there, gave a different version: that Alexander pulled the pin out of the pole, which let him slide the yoke off, which exposed the ends of the cord, which could then simply be unwound. The pin says: I looked at the whole assembly instead of at the part everyone was staring at.

Both are refusals to keep pulling. Both are recognitions that when the end is buried, effort is not the missing ingredient.

---

Which brings me back to the splice, and then I'll stop.

If you need two ropes to be one rope, and you need it to be strong, you do not tie them together. You unlay them. You open the twisted strands of each end, and you tuck the strands of one into the body of the other, over and under, in the pattern the rope already uses, so that the two ropes' own helices continue into each other. Then you roll it under your foot, and load it, and the strands settle, and after a while you cannot see where the join is. A good splice retains something like ninety percent of the rope's original strength, against sixty or seventy for the best knot.

It works because it isn't a knot. A knot holds by pinching the rope against itself, concentrating force at a bend. A splice holds by *becoming the rope*. There is no bend, no pinch point, no place where the load has to turn a corner. The two things have interpenetrated along their length and the distinction between them has been dissolved rather than bridged. It takes far longer than tying. It requires you to temporarily destroy the structure of both ends. You have to unmake the rope a little to make it continuous.

I don't think I need to say what this is a metaphor for. That's the trouble with good metaphors — they arrive already knowing what they mean, and the only respectful thing is to leave them alone and let the reader do the last tuck.

So: the rabbit comes out of the hole, runs around the tree, goes back down the hole. You pull it tight. It will hold your weight, and it will come undone in one motion when you want it to, even after it has held everything you could put on it. That combination — grips absolutely under load, releases instantly when slack — is not something you can get from a mechanism. You get it from a shape. Somebody found that shape, probably by accident, probably several thousand years ago, probably in more than one place, and it has been passed hand to hand ever since, mostly without words, and it is still, right now, the best answer to a question that everyone who has ever needed to fasten a rope to a post has asked.

Nobody knows who found it. There is no name on it. It's just a good shape that human hands remember.

It requires you to temporarily destroy the structure of both ends. You have to unmake the rope a little to make it continuous.

I don't think I need to say what this is a metaphor for. That's the trouble with good metaphors — they arrive already knowing what they mean, and the only respectful thing is to leave them alone and let the reader do the last tuck.

So: the rabbit comes out of the hole, runs around the tree, goes back down the hole. You pull it tight. It will hold your weight, and it will come undone in one motion when you want it to, even after it has held everything you could put on it. That combination — grips absolutely under load, releases instantly when slack — is not something you can get from a mechanism. You get it from a shape. Somebody found that shape, probably by accident, probably several thousand years ago, probably in more than one place, and it has been passed hand to hand ever since, mostly without words, and it is still, right now, the best answer to a question that everyone who has ever needed to fasten a rope to a post has asked.

Nobody knows who found it. There is no name on it. It's just a good shape that human hands remember.
